issues.title: Security Considerations: Post-Compromise Security
issues.author: dennisjackson
issues.body:
8.1 of draft-thomson-webpush-sym states: 

> This message encryption scheme does not provide confidentiality of messages that are sent after a key becomes compromised. A key compromise leads to loss of confidentiality for all messages sent under the same key, in the past or future. 

This is also true of draft-thomson-webpush-hpke for the server's HPKE key. Both systems only achieve forward secrecy once the server's long term key material is destroyed and only achieve post compromise security when the keys have been (securely) rotated.

When thinking about the different properties between the two schemes, I think it's the lack of forward secrecy with respect to the client compromise that separates the two. Once a client has done a HPKE encap it can throw away the old secret, but the symmetric client has to keep that secret around. 

In light of the overhead of PQ HPKE and all the other things that go wrong when clients get compromised, it probably makes sense to go for the symmetric option and try to bake in a good rotation flow?

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
> This is also true of draft-thomson-webpush-hpke for the server's HPKE key. 

I think you might have this a little backwards.  In the HPKE-based design -- and the present one, which is also asymmetric -- the client is the one that holds a long term key.  The expectation is that the server is generating a fresh ephemeral key for every message.  My understanding is that this is necessary, otherwise you get a two-time pad under either asymmetric design.

> When thinking about the different properties between the two schemes, I think it's the lack of forward secrecy with respect to the client compromise that separates the two. Once a client has done a HPKE encap it can throw away the old secret, but the symmetric client has to keep that secret around.

Flip that around and then I think it's right.  That is indeed the problem I'm concerned with.  A server that sends messages to many clients, if it were compromised, no messages are revealed in the present design, but a server compromise risks every message it ever sent if we move to a symmetric key.  Obviously, clients that hold long term keys are a risk to every message they have ever received (and might receive for some time) if they are compromised, but those are a diverse and distributed population and each has to be compromised separately.  That makes me less concerned.

Does that inversion change your conclusion at all?

comments.author: dennisjackson
comments.body:
Doh. Yeah I did indeed have it backwards. 

> The expectation is that the server is generating a fresh ephemeral key for every message. My understanding is that this is necessary, otherwise you get a two-time pad under either asymmetric design.

Once you've derived a shared secret, why can't you retain a counter as a state and symmetrically encrypt until you want to retire the key or counter? That lets you amortize the cost over of the asymmetric key exchange over multiple messages. 

> > When thinking about the different properties between the two schemes, I think it's the lack of forward secrecy with respect to the client compromise that separates the two. Once a client has done a HPKE encap it can throw away the old secret, but the symmetric client has to keep that secret around.
> 
> Flip that around and then I think it's right. [...] Does that inversion change your conclusion at all? 

Gotcha. You could achieve forward secrecy in a purely symmetric design by ratcheting the key forwards. The server stores `epoch || key` and on every messages will increment epoch and replace `key` with `KDF(key)` after every encryption. The client can store `oldest_acceptable _epoch || key` and ratchet less aggressively (if it needs to tolerate delayed or out of order messages). 

That essentially bakes in key rotation and clients can enforce it. The post-compromise security is weaker than the asymmetric version, but I think in this setting that's probably not such a big deal?    

Maybe overall you want the hybrid approach of letting servers do an infrequent asymmetric key exchange to setup a state and then use a ratchet to ensure PFS for the lifetime of that state? That might make life easier for server operators since they can put the client's asymmetric key material in long-lived global state and individual servers can derive keys as they need them and keep their session state locally - allowing graceful failover etc.

comments.author: martinthomson
comments.body:
> Once you've derived a shared secret, why can't you retain a counter as a state and symmetrically encrypt until you want to retire the key or counter? That lets you amortize the cost over of the asymmetric key exchange over multiple messages.

Web Push is supposed to be used to initiate richer communication: the server sends a single small message to a browser to wake it up.  The browser then initiates direct communication over TLS.  So there should not be any pattern of multiple messages involved.  At least not to the extent that you would benefit from establishing a session.

> You could achieve forward secrecy in a purely symmetric design by ratcheting the key forwards. 

I really should forward my conversation with @davidben, who suggested almost exactly the same design.  Though yours is a little better, I think.  The limitations are, I hope, obvious.  Forward secrecy, not post-compromise secrecy.  Though your point is well-taken: a ratchet on the server protects old messages in the event of server compromise.  It does nothing for future messages, though perhaps that is also true no matter what cryptography is used.

The client-side compromise looks fairly similar to what we have today, because they have to hold fairly old keys for extended periods, but they can ratchet forwards when they receive a new epoch, so maybe it is even better than today from that angle [^1].

[^1]: Not that client compromise is something to really worry about given that they are likely holding a lot more than a few keys: they often hold the plaintext of all those messages.  Along with the credentials used with the site, ...

All told, I think that iterating on the symmetric design to include a ratchet is very reasonable.  It costs a few extra bytes, but it might save more by removing the need for the explicit nonce if you move from "epoch" to "sequence number".  That leaves the design as something like:

```
secret[i] = KDF(k[i-1], "secret")
key[i] = KDF(k[i-1], "key")
nonce[i] = KDF(k[i-1], "nonce")
message = i || AEAD(key[i], nonce[i], aad, pt)
```

The API returns a tuple of the secret (which needs to be large enough to feed the KDF properly) and the *current* sequence number.

Because each is per-site, this is very simple if you assume in-order delivery.  Even without that, a client can remember the secrets necessary to fill in gaps if it likes. Though I would strongly recommend capping the time or number of messages past such a gap.

Not sure if it is necessary to have anything other than empty AAD, but that would be the only question I have.  The belt and braces version folds in the sequence number.
